RNAi specialist Alnylam Pharmaceuticals will advance the Huntington’s disease drug brezosiran into a placebo-controlled study in 2027 once regulatory alignment is achieved.
Alnylam is eyeing a pivotal trial for a Huntington’s disease drug after an early-stage clinical study showed “robust” reductions in the key huntingtin protein that is known to drive the difficult neurodegenerative disease.
If the therapy is ultimately approved, Alnylam could find itself with a multibillion-dollar opportunity in Huntington’s disease (HD), Oppenheimer wrote on Friday. “The severity of HD, coupled with lack of treatments, confers a significant market opportunity,” the analyst said.
In an ongoing Phase 1b clinical trial, ALN-HTT02—now to be known as brezosiran—spurred what the company called robust and dose-dependent reductions in mutant huntingtin protein (mHTT) in the cerebrospinal fluid. This was confirmed with two independent assays, Alnylam said in a Friday press release .
The data were presented in a poster at the European Huntington’s Disease Network Clinical Research Congress in Krakow, Poland. The drug is part of a longtime partnership with Regeneron, which was initially signed in 2019 and is worth upward of $1 billion.
The highest dose group saw a mean reduction of 60%–64% at three months, with the highest observed reduction reaching 83%.
The results fall in Oppenheimer’s “best case scenario,” suggesting “best-in-class knockdown,” the firm said in a Friday morning note.
But the data are early, and Alnylam did not reveal any information on the potential clinical efficacy because the follow-up period was too short, the firm noted. Stifel analysts also noted that there are many questions to be answered—and in the tough Huntington’s space, early clinical results don’t always mean the program will succeed.
“While these early results do look interesting/positive, there’s still clinical risk here in that Roche’s tominersen also demonstrated favorable CSF mHTT-lowering, which didn’t translate to a benefit,” the firm wrote on Friday morning. Roche has since abandoned the antisense oligonucleotide asset. “From a stock perspective, we know from others in HD it can take a while to prove out clinical benefit.”
Still, Alnylam was encouraged enough by the early readout to advance the program.
“The observed durability of mHTT-lowering shows the potential for a twice-yearly dosing paradigm in downstream development,” Alnylam said.
The RNAi specialist will move brezosiran into a placebo-controlled study in 2027 once regulatory alignment is achieved, according to Friday’s news release.

“We plan to evaluate our differentiated huntingtin-lowering approach in a rigorous placebo-controlled study to determine whether it can alter the course of Huntington’s disease,” Pushkal Garg, Alnylam’s Chief Research and Development Officer, said in a statement.
Brezosiran is an RNAi therapeutic developed using Alnylam’s C16 conjugate platform that aids delivery into the central nervous system. The therapy targets exon 1 of the huntingtin (HTT) mRNA transcript, which is designed to reduce production of all forms of the protein, differentiating the asset from other HD drug candidates.
Brezosiran was flagged by analysts earlier this year as a potential morale booster after the company had to cut guidance. While exciting, Stifel wants to see more from the Huntington’s program before weighing in on whether it will be a future growth driver.
“As we see it, this offers promising proof-of-concept—good safety, strong knockdown—but for the stock it’ll likely take more data to earn significant credit here, especially as we’re at a pivotal point in the TTR launch where the next couple quarters are important for investors seeing that the franchise is on track to meet ALNY’s 2030/long-term goals,” the firm wrote. Alnylam’s stock was steady around $224.54 apiece on Friday morning.
The company will present the Phase 1b Huntington’s data during a roundtable event on October 26.
Huntington’s disease is one of the toughest spaces in biopharma, with many failed assets and approaches littering the path . UniQure inspired hope last year when the gene therapy ifezuntirgene inilparvovec showed a 75% three-year slowing of the disease at three years in September 2025. That response rate has since narrowed , with more recent data showing a 44% slowing of disease progression at four years. The asset has nevertheless been filed for approval with the FDA.

source_document.body:
The Port of Coos Bay has secured nearly $205 million in federal funding to upgrade its rail line, advancing a proposed Oregon container terminal that would rely on trains to move cargo between ships and inland markets.
The $204.8 million award, announced Oct. 19 by Oregon Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden and Rep. Val Hoyle, will fund final design and construction of improvements to the Coos Bay Rail Line. The work is intended to increase capacity, improve reliability and prepare the railroad to support the proposed Pacific Coast Intermodal Port, or PCIP.
The funding comes through the U.S. Department of Transportation ’s Consolidated Rail Infrastructure and Safety Improvements (CRISI) grants program. Planned improvements include repairing and replacing track, ties, bridges and tunnels, according to Hoyle’s office.
The 111-mile railroad runs from Coos Bay to near Eugene. Its rehabilitation is a critical component of the broader port development, which would create a deepwater container terminal with a ship-to-rail connection.
It’s the first large construction grant for PCIP, which plans significant improvements to handle container volumes.
Port officials described the award as a major step toward developing another West Coast container gateway.
Kyle Stevens, president of the Oregon International Port of Coos Bay Board of Commissioners, in a statement said the money puts the project “on a path toward constructing the critical rail infrastructure needed to bring a new West Coast container gateway to life.”
The award follows more than $11 million in federal Port Infrastructure Development Program funding announced earlier this year for the Coos Bay rail project, according to the congressional delegation.
The proposed terminal, which would compete for regional business with Portland, Ore., Seattle and Tacoma, Wash., as well as Vancouver and Prince Rupert in western Canada, has a price tag of more than $2 billion and remains years away from opening pending additional funding, permitting and environmental reviews. Development also comes as shifting U.S. tariff and trade policy has seen more headhaul container traffic from Asia routed away from Pacific Northwest hubs and through the British Columbia gateways, for entry into the Midwest U.S. via intermodal rail.
Before the latest award, the project had attracted approximately $70 million in federal funding through four grant programs, along with $160 million from Oregon. NorthPoint Development, the private company slated to operate the container terminal, has invested $25 million, according to local media.
Supporters say the development could generate 2,500 permanent jobs and another 2,500 temporary construction jobs, helping diversify a regional economy affected by the timber industry’s decline. Environmental advocates have raised concerns about dredging and its effects on wildlife, with opponents favoring greater emphasis on industries such as healthcare and tourism.
The project’s next steps include selecting contractors to assist with permitting and review. Proposals are due Oct. 28, followed by environmental reviews and opportunities for public comment.

Pristine 1967 Dodge Coronet R/T Has a Rare Feature in Plain Sight
18 photos
Photo: basilclassiccars.com
The Dodge Coronet was first introduced in 1949 as a full-size car , but it's mainly iconic for the years it spent in the intermediate market. Discontinued in 1959, the Coronet returned in 1965 as a mid-size car. It was part of the muscle car wars and used as a base for two of Dodge's most iconic models, the Charger and Super Bee.
The Coronet is obviously overshadowed by the other two Mopars. But that's not to say that the Coronet is not a proper muscle car with the right features. Sure, most of the vehicles sold were mundane sedans and station wagons, but the two-door models were available with Chrysler's hottest golden-era mill, the 426-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) Hemi V8.
And here's a fact that many of us tend to forget: the Coronet was the very first Dodge to feature the R/T badge. We often associate the emblem with the Charger, which got it in 1968, but the Coronet R/T arrived a year earlier. It was only available as a two-door hardtop and convertible and came standard with the 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) RB, available only with a four-barrel carburetor at the time.
The Hemi was on the R/T's options list, while transmission choices included the three-speed TorqueFlite automatic and the four-speed manual. 1970 was the final year for the Coronet R/T. In 1971, Dodge redesigned the Coronet as a four-door model only, with the Super Bee version moved on the Charger platform.
As Dodge's bread-and-butter intermediate, the Coronet was quite popular overall. However, only a small fraction of these cars were ordered in R/T specs. Specifically, Dodge sold over 700,000 units between 1967 and 1970, but only 30,896 examples were R/T cars. That's less than 5% of the total output.
Two thirds of these R/Ts were sold in the first two model years. The numbers split almost evenly, with 10,181 delivered in 1967. The blue example you see here is one of those cars, but it's not as common as the production number suggests. This Mopar has a rare factory feature in plain sight; I'm talking about the convertible top.
You see, while most mid-size cars were available in this body style at the time, drop tops were far from popular. This feature alone puts the Coronet R/T into three-digit territory, as Dodge sold only 628 cars. And needless to say, the blue-on-blue color combo makes it even rarer (the soft top is white, so no triple-blue treatment here).
The Mopar packs the 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) RB rated at 375 horsepower, which was the standard mill. It mates with a three-speed TorqueFlite automatic. It's unclear how many were ordered with this transmission, but we're probably looking at under 400 examples.
Rarity aside, this Coronet R/T is a gem. The car has been restored and looks flawless inside and out, while the engine bay is equally clean. And it's also notably more affordable than a Hemi. source_document.body:
Emerson’s Rosemount Annubar technology preserves valuable process energy by delivering reliable flow measurement in demanding liquid, steam, and gas applications.
Differential pressure (DP) flow measurement remains one of the most widely used technologies in power generation, utilizing the pressure difference created by a primary element installed within a pipe. Various DP technologies are available, each offering unique advantages and tradeoffs in accuracy, pressure loss, installation requirements, and cost. Among these, averaging Pitot tubes have gained increasing adoption due to their exceptionally low permanent pressure loss (PPL) and economy in large diameter piping.
Unlike a single-point Pitot tube—which measures velocity at a single location and therefore, has potential for accuracy degradation in non-ideal flow profiles—an averaging Pitot tube integrates pressure measurements from multiple sensing ports distributed across the pipe diameter. This design improves accuracy in large pipes and non-ideal flow conditions while maintaining low PPL compared to traditional DP primary elements, such as flow nozzles or orifice plates.
Modern Approach to Traditional Flow Measurement
DP flow measurement requires the creation of a restriction within the flowing fluid. Traditionally, this was achieved using a primary element, such as an orifice plate, which introduces a restriction that generates a measurable pressure differential. Orifice meters are widely used due to their simplicity, proven performance, and high accuracy. However, creating this restriction permanently removes energy from the process. Every pound per square inch (psi) of pressure loss represents energy that the plant has already paid to create through pumps, fans, or steam generation. Once that pressure is dissipated across the primary element, it cannot be recovered and is no longer available to move fluids, transfer heat, or support downstream processes.
In steam lines, this also means less energy available to the turbine, which raises heat rate. To maintain required operating conditions, the lost pressure must be restored through additional pumping or fan power, increasing auxiliary power consumption, fuel consumption, and net plant heat rate. In effect, PPL not only reduces the useful energy available, but it also creates an ongoing energy penalty that the plant must continually pay for over the life of the installation. In many applications, removing this energy penalty can offset the initial investment in the Rosemount Annubar flow meter (Figure 1).
1. The Rosemount Annubar uses multiple sensing ports distributed across the pipe diameter to capture a representative average of the flow profile. By measuring the differential between impact (high pressure) and stagnation (low pressure), it provides an accurate flow measurement, while creating minimal disruption to the process. Courtesy: Emerson
Many power applications—such as circulating and cooling water, steam lines, combustion air, flue gas, and gas turbine inlet ducting—involve large pipe diameters, where minimizing pressure loss is critical to reducing operating costs. As line sizes increase, an integrated Annubar flow meter becomes an attractive alternative to traditional DP solutions. Conventional solutions require cutting the pipe, welding flanges, and installing impulse piping, increasing procurement and installation complexity as well as maintenance needs.
In contrast, an integrated Annubar flow meter combines the averaging Pitot tube (APT) primary element and DP transmitter into a complete, factory-assembled solution that simplifies installation and commissioning. In addition, installation can become expensive in large diameter piping systems, and achieving accurate measurements typically requires long lengths of straight pipe both upstream and downstream of the meter. Unlike many traditional flow technologies, the Annubar multi-port design averages the flow profile across the pipe diameter. This reduces its sensitivity to flow disturbances caused by elbows, dampers, valves, and other upstream piping or ductwork, allowing accurate measurement with shorter straight-run requirements, and providing greater installation flexibility.
The Rosemount 485 Annubar Primary Element has a distinctive T-shaped profile (Figure 2), engineered to deliver reliable performance in demanding process conditions. The flat leading edge creates a stable impact pressure zone that deflects particles away from the slots, reducing the risk of plugging and maintaining measurement in applications with entrained particulates, such as fly ash.
2. By maximizing the measurable differential pressure while minimizing permanent pressure loss, Annubar’s T-shaped design delivers reliable flow measurement with lower lifetime energy costs. Courtesy: Emerson
Unlike traditional APT designs that rely on a single low-pressure port that is susceptible to fouling and flow disturbances, the Annubar utilizes multiple stagnation ports. This design improves measurement accuracy, enhances signal stability, and makes the Annubar less sensitive to flow irregularities than cylindrical shapes. For gas and steam applications, the integrated thermowell allows direct installation of a resistance temperature detector (RTD) within the assembly, providing an accurate process temperature measurement at the same location as the flow measurement. By combining flow and temperature sensing into a single pipe penetration, the integrated 485 Annubar flow meter simplifies installation, reduces leak points, lowers installation costs, and improves mass flow accuracy through more precise temperature compensation.
For more severe applications, such as main steam lines, the Rosemount 585 Annubar Primary Element for Severe Service (Figure 3) extends Annubar technology to the high-temperature, high-pressure, and high-velocity conditions found between the boiler or heat recovery steam generator (HRSG) and the steam turbine. Its robust construction is designed for severe service, while retaining the core advantages of direct flow measurement, low PPL, and ease of installation.
3. The Rosemount 585 Annubar Primary Element for Severe Service is engineered for main steam service and other critical applications. Courtesy: Emerson
While conventional DP or other flow technologies may be more practical in small line sizes, the advantages of the Annubar increase significantly as pipe diameter grows. As line size increases, the combined impact of lower installation costs and reduced energy losses make the Annubar increasingly cost effective (Figure 4).
4. As line size increases, the total installed and operating cost of traditional orifice plates rises rapidly due to equipment costs and increased energy losses from PPL. The low PPL design of the Rosemount Annubar delivers substantially lower lifecycle costs. Courtesy: Emerson
The Annubar is particularly attractive for large-diameter-pipe, balance-of-plant, and utility systems; steam distribution networks; circulating and cooling water systems; and combustion air or flue gas flow measurement in ducts or stacks. Available for line sizes up to 96 inches, the Annubar is an effective and economical solution in applications where installation constraints, pressure loss, or pipe size limit the viability of alternative flow technologies.
The Annubar simplifies installation through its insertion style design, requiring only a single pipe penetration rather than pipe cutting, flanges, and extensive impulse piping. A variety of mounting configurations allow installation flexibility, including flanged, Pak-Lok compression, and Flo-Tap retractable designs to accommodate different process conditions and piping requirements.
Flo-Tap designs can be installed or retracted under pressure without a unit outage. No spool section is required, although Emerson offers one for a drop in solution. Together, these installation options reduce engineering complexity, minimize outage time, and lower total installed cost compared to conventional DP flow meter designs (Figure 5).
5. The Rosemount 4051SFA Annubar Flow Meter combines a Rosemount 485 Annubar primary element with a Rosemount 4051S differential pressure transmitter and integrated temperature measurement in a compact assembly. By mounting the transmitter directly to the sensor, the integrated solution eliminates the impulse lines commonly required in traditional DP flow meter installations. Courtesy: Emerson
To illustrate these advantages in practice, the following three power plant case studies show how Annubar flow meters improved measurement performance while reducing installation, maintenance, and lifecycle costs.
Optimizing Combustion Air Flow Control
A coal-fired power plant was working to improve combustion efficiency, reduce emissions, and lower fuel consumption, but it had no reliable method for measuring combustion air flow. Instead, operators estimated airflow from induced draft (ID) fan performance curves, producing errors of ±25% to 30%. In a balanced-draft pulverized-coal boiler, combustion air is supplied by the forced draft (FD) fan and primary air (PA) fans. FD air feeds the furnace as secondary combustion air, while PA air dries and conveys pulverized coal to the burners.
The ID fan, located downstream of the furnace, pulls flue gas through the boiler and out the stack, maintaining a slightly negative furnace pressure. Thus, air-side fans (FD/PA) handle combustion air intake, while the ID fan handles exhaust flue gas. As engineers worked to optimize combustion by balancing air flow, fuel flow, flue gas oxygen levels, and stack emissions, the absence of accurate airflow measurement limited their ability to precisely control the process and achieve peak boiler performance.
The main combustion air inlet is delivered through a 4-ft x 5-ft duct, creating a significant flow measurement challenge. The plant required an accurate and economical method to measure airflow across this large cross-sectional area without adding significant pressure loss. Complicating matters further, the duct contained multiple elbows and limited straight-run piping, resulting in a highly disturbed flow profile, making conventional point measurement techniques unreliable. Obtaining an accurate airflow measurement required a technology capable of averaging velocity across the duct, while maintaining low PPL.
Emerson engineers recommended a pair of Rosemount 485 Annubar Primary Elements as a cost-effective way to solve the challenge. The sensors were installed parallel to one another across the short dimension of the duct, allowing them to sample a broad portion of the velocity profile. By averaging pressure measurements from multiple sensing points, the Annubar provided a representative flow measurement despite the disturbed flow conditions created by the duct’s multiple elbows and limited straight-run length.
Because the installation did not provide the straight-run lengths typically required for a fully developed flow profile and the large 4-ft × 5-ft duct exhibited significant velocity variations across its cross section, Emerson also recommended performing a Pitot tube traverse to characterize the flow profile. Engineers used a single-point Pitot tube to measure velocity at multiple locations throughout the duct and under a range of operating conditions, creating a detailed map of the airflow distribution.
This data was then used to establish a site-specific flow coefficient (K factor) that accounted for the unique installation effects. By combining the dual Annubar installation with the flow profile characterization, the plant achieved airflow measurement accuracy of approximately ±5%, a substantial improvement over the previous ±25% to 30% estimates. With reliable airflow data available, engineers were able to more effectively optimize the air-to-fuel ratio, improve combustion efficiency, and reduce emissions.
With improved data, the plant achieved many positive results:
Verified 10% reduction in fuel consumption.
Reduced combustion air flow lowered stack losses, improving boiler efficiency and net heat rate.
Reduced demand on the FD and ID fans, lowering auxiliary (parasitic) power consumption and increasing net unit output.
Preserving Main Steam Pressure
During a combined-cycle upgrade at a power plant, traditional flow nozzles on the main steam lines were replaced with Rosemount 585 Annubar Primary Element for Severe Service flow meters. The primary drivers were easier maintenance and significantly lower PPL. Unlike flow nozzles, which can be difficult to remove and often require spool piece modifications during maintenance, Annubar sensors can be inserted and retracted more easily, reducing maintenance complexity and downtime.
The most significant benefit, however, was the reduction in PPL. The existing flow nozzles created a permanent pressure loss of approximately 8.2 psi of steam pressure, while the Annubar reduced this to just 0.73 psi, an improvement of more than 11:1. Because steam pressure represents energy the plant has already paid to generate, preserving that pressure leaves more energy available to drive the turbine, improving heat rate and net output rather than pressure being lost across the flowmeter.
After one year of operation, the customer determined the reduction in PPL delivered approximately $43,000 in annual savings through increased power generation and improved efficiency (Figure 6).
6. The project achieved a payback period of less than one year, demonstrating the economic value of minimizing PPL in high-energy steam applications. In addition, simplified maintenance and installation allowed easier insertion and removal of the sensor without the costly piping modifications often required for flow nozzles. Courtesy: Emerson
Local Steam Distribution
A power plant that supplies steam to a nearby industrial park needed an accurate and reliable method to measure steam mass and energy flow for revenue-grade billing. Their customers pay according to use, requiring metering that both sides accept as valid for billing. As the steam distribution network expanded in size and complexity, maintaining measurement while minimizing pressure loss and installation costs became an increasingly significant challenge.
This power plant had been using DP flow meters of its own design, but they tended to be maintenance-intensive due to frequent impulse line leaks. These flow meters were positioned at customer sites, frequently miles from the source, making real-time delivery of consumption data dependent on long and maintenance intensive cables. Recognizing the importance of accurate steam energy measurement for customer billing, the utility elected to modernize the entire infrastructure serving all 20 customers to improve reliability, accuracy, and long-term operating efficiency.
To address these challenges, Emerson engineers developed a comprehensive metering solution featuring the Rosemount 3051SFA MultiVariable Flow Meter. The integrated design eliminated the impulse lines that had been a frequent source of maintenance and reliability issues, while providing accurate measurements of flow, pressure, and temperature required for steam energy calculations. The remaining challenge was collecting data from customer sites distributed throughout the industrial park without relying on extensive cabling infrastructure.
The need for cables was eliminated by adding an Emerson Wireless 775 THUM Adapter, enabling WirelessHART communication to a centralized gateway. Each metering assembly combined a Rosemount 485 Annubar Primary Element with a Rosemount 3051S MultiVariable Pressure Transmitter, measuring differential pressure, static pressure, and process temperature in a single device while dynamically calculating steam mass flow 22 times per second within the transmitter.
All measurement data was transmitted through a single WirelessHART signal and routed via General Packet Radio Services (GPRS) to the utility’s distributed control system (DCS), creating a robust wireless steam metering network, with minimal infrastructure and maintenance requirements. By consolidating real time flow and energy consumption data from all 20 customers, the utility gained greater visibility into steam distribution, improved billing accuracy, and enhanced overall management of steam energy resources.
Evaluating Flow Measurement Opportunities
When analyzing the lifecycle costs of a flow measurement solution, end users should consider not only the initial purchase and installation costs, but also the ongoing energy costs associated with PPL. While some pressure loss is unavoidable with most flow measurement types, selecting technologies that minimize flow disruption can significantly reduce operating expenses over the life of the installation. The applications presented in this article demonstrate how Rosemount Annubar flow meters provide accurate and reliable flow measurement, while reducing installation complexity, maintenance requirements, and energy consumption.
Due to its inherently low pipe blockage, the Rosemount Annubar flow meter can significantly improve system efficiency when replacing traditional technologies. By preserving valuable fluid and steam energy that would otherwise be lost across restrictive primary elements, the Annubar reduces fuel consumption, pumping and fan power costs, and overall operating expenses. These energy savings, combined with simplified installation and reduced maintenance requirements, often result in a substantially lower total cost of ownership, while helping plants improve heat rate and maximize available net output.
—Kassandra McDougall is a global product manager at Emerson. She is responsible for managing Emerson’s DP Flow portfolio.

Shares of refrigerated carrier Marten Transport were down 7% in midday trading on Friday, following a disappointing third-quarter report. Despite improving supply-demand fundamentals, a runup in fuel and health insurance costs, among other items, were a drag in the period.
Table: Marten’s key performance indictors – Consolidated
Mondovi, Wisconsin-based Marten ( NASDAQ: MRTN ) reported net income of $2.9 million, or 4 cents per share, for the third quarter. The result was a penny higher than the year-ago quarter but 2 cents light of the consensus estimate.
The company said higher fuel and payroll costs, including driver pay increases, were only partially offset by an increase in gains on equipment sales. The net impact was a $3.7-million hit to net income, or 4.5 cents per share.
Consolidated revenue of $223 million was 1% higher year over year. The 2025 sale of its intermodal unit to Hub Group ( NASDAQ: HUBG ) presented a $9.9-million revenue headwind during the quarter.
Table: Marten’s key performance indictors – Truckload & Dedicated
One-way truckload revenue increased 12% y/y to $117 million. Excluding fuel surcharges, revenue was up 4% y/y as revenue per tractor per week (ex-fuel) increased 15% on a 9% smaller fleet.
Marten has been managing truck counts to improve asset utilization. Deadhead was down 30 basis points y/y to 10.7%. Revenue per loaded mile (ex-fuel) increased 14% y/y to $3.02. The unit was unprofitable at a 100.2% operating ratio (ex-fuel), 200 bps better y/y, but 280 bps worse sequentially.
SONAR: Reefer Outbound Tender Rejection Index (ROTRI.USA) for 2026 (blue shaded area), 2025 (yellow line), 2024 (green line) and 2023 (pink line). A proxy for truck capacity, the reefer tender rejection index shows the number of loads being rejected by carriers. Current tender rejections show a tight truckload market. To learn more about SONAR, click here .
The dedicated segment reported a 9% y/y decline in revenue (ex-fuel) as an 11% decline in the truck count was only partially offset by a 2% increase in revenue per tractor (ex-fuel). Revenue per loaded mile (ex-fuel) was down 2% y/y to $2.41. The unit logged a 97.6% OR (ex-fuel), 360 bps worse y/y and 220 bps worse sequentially.
(Marten does not host a quarterly call.)
“The truckload freight market has sharply tightened since earlier this year as renewed and enhanced enforcement of federal and state law is removing a meaningful amount of noncompliant and unqualified driver capacity from the marketplace,” said Randy Marten, chairman and CEO, in a news release. “We are securing higher pricing from our customers for our premium services while enhancing freight quality across our network within these early stages of the freight market upcycle.”
Table: Marten’s key performance indictors – Brokerage
Brokerage revenue was flat y/y at $39 million as a 15% decline in shipments was offset by a 17% increase in revenue per load. The unit’s OR improved 110 bps to 94.8%, flat with the 2026 second quarter .
Cash flow from operations was $83 million in the first nine months of 2026, a 5% y/y decline. The company maintained a debt-free balance sheet in the period.
The average age of its tractor fleet was 2.5 years compared to 2.2 years in the year-ago quarter.
Shares of MRTN are down 37% since a mid-June peak.
Why it matters? Marten Transport is viewed as a “refrigerated pure play.” It is the only public carrier in the reefer market and its quarterly results serve as a bellwether for the industry.

LEGO Ideas Alfa Romeo Montreal Mirrors the Best Italian Car That Launched at the Worst Possible Time
12 photos
Photo: LEGO Ideas/Musstrafaccatrator
No matter how big the passion for automobiles some people have, the majority of them would probably have a hard time trying to remember what the Alfa Romeo Montreal is. Nobody can blame them for that, of course, but this reality makes the LEGO Ideas set we have here even more surprising.
The Montreal was born as a concept car on request for the 1967 Universal Exposition held in the namesake Canadian city. Put together in just nine months, it was penned by Bertone's Marcello Gandini and used a Giulia Sprint GT as a base.
There were several things setting this streamlined coupe apart from pretty much everything else that was available at the time: a low radiator grille, headlights half-concealed by the car's hood, making them look like eyes with eyelids, the two long doors , and the almost horizontal glass at the rear.
For the purpose of the 1967 Universal Exposition, Alfa Romeo only put together two Montreals, which were proudly displayed at the main entrance and, thanks to a clever play of mirrors, repeatedly transported inside the exhibition space.
The concepts proved quite the hit among those attending, so Alfa decided to make it for the masses. That's how a production version was quickly conceived, using technologies from cars such as the 33 Stradale and a series of design changes meant to be more user-friendly, if you will.
The car would have probably been a huge hit if it weren't for the troubles that defined the early 1970s. Shown at the 1970 Geneva International Motor Show, the production Montreal started rolling off the lines two years later.
A few years after that, with just 3,925 units produced by 1977, the same production lines stopped, on account of the oil crisis and the public's interest in such cars plummeting into the abyss.
The LEGO Ideas set I stumbled upon these days tries to bring back the Montreal, this time in plastic brick form. The work of a fan designer who goes by the name Musstrafaccatrator, the set comes to life after an unspecified number of parts are properly assembled, forming a design that comes with a working steering system, opening doors, trunk and hood, and a replica of a V8 engine under the hood.
The set was submitted for public voting in the summer of last year, and it has gained 3,053 backers since that time. It only has 141 days left to get to 5,000 and get an extension before an official evaluation can be performed when double that number is reached.
Until we get to learn if the Montreal is coming back as a LEGO set or not, there's always the option to go see the two real-life prototypes in their pearl white overalls. That's because the concepts are now part of the FCA Heritage collection, displayed at the Alfa Romeo History Museum in Milan, Italy.

source_document.body:
A tanker carrying 40,000 metric tons of Russian diesel is heading for New York under a new U.S.-Russia supply agreement , marking a reopening of a trade curtailed by Washington’s 2022 ban on Russian oil and petroleum imports.
The Malta-flagged Agioi Fanendes loaded ultra-low-sulfur diesel at Primorsk, Russia’s Baltic Sea oil port, on Oct. 22 and is expected to arrive in the United States Nov. 7, according to LSEG ship-tracking data cited by Reuters. The buyer and seller were not immediately identified.
The voyage is the first identified U.S.-bound shipment under the agreement President Donald Trump announced Oct. 9. It’s reported to be the first U.S. import since the 2022 ban, Reuters reported, although AP quoted maritime analyst Kpler states that it would be the first Russian diesel delivery since July 2023. Reuters cited LSEG shipping data for the current voyage, but does not identify the last previous delivery or give its arrival date. The AP report does not name the vessel, discharge port or circumstances of that 2023 cargo.
The diesel-specific sanctions relief is under General License 135, issued October 9, 2026, by the Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). It temporarily authorizes Russian-diesel transactions otherwise prohibited under two sanctions programs: the Russian Harmful Foreign Activities Sanctions Regulations, 31 CFR Part 587, and the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations, 31 CFR Part 589.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed Friday to Reuters that the first tanker under the arrangement had departed and said regular supplies would follow. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak has said additional shipments are planned as Russian and U.S. companies finalize delivery contracts.
The agreement combines U.S. sanctions relief with Russia’s decision to lift its own restrictions on diesel exports. Trump announced an initial release of 300,000 metric tons to U.S. and global markets, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter,” according to Trump’s executive order .
The shipment comes as Trump seeks to rein in soaring diesel prices ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Its scheduled arrival, however, falls after Election Day.
“The diesel deal shows that Washington’s Russia policy is now driven by high prices at the pump before the November 3 midterm elections, rather than by any shared trans-Atlantic strategy,” said Matthias Matthijs, senior fellow for Europe at the Council on Foreign Relations.
Mohit Kumar, chief European economist at Jefferies, in an Oct. 12 research note quoted by CNBC, wrote, “Trump is exploring all avenues to bring down diesel prices before the mid-terms.”
At roughly 300,000 barrels, the cargo represents about 7% of the approximately 4 million barrels of diesel consumed by the U.S. economy each day, according to AP. Energy policy experts cited by the news agency said the import agreement was unlikely to substantially reduce fuel prices.
The agreement has drawn criticism from Ukraine, which has urged its partners to tighten restrictions on Russian energy revenue as Putin presses his war against Kyiv. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the U.S. decision “a weak decision by strong partners,” AP reported.
Why it matters: The sanctions relief makes Russian diesel easier to trade and transport, potentially increasing Moscow’s export earnings, while offering an uncertain benefit to fuel buyers.
This article was updated Oct. 23 to add details on the last pre-sanction oil shipments, and analyst commentary on the political reason for the sanction relief. A link was also added to the text of Trump’s executive order.

Following the withdrawal of billions of dollars in investments from Boehringer Ingelheim and Eli Lilly, German lawmakers have proposed a clause to the country’s healthcare reforms set to take effect Jan. 1.
Roche has identified a recently introduced legislative proposal as the “final opportunity” for Germany to recover from policies that have caused multiple companies to pause planned investments in the country.
Basel-based Roche put investment decisions in Germany on hold this summer, the Financial Times reported in August. Daniel Steiners, head of Roche Germany, expanded on the decision this week in an interview with German newspaper Welt , accusing policymakers of destroying trust. A Roche spokesperson attributed the investment pause to recent German healthcare reforms.
“The legislation imposes a substantial burden on Germany’s research-based pharmaceutical industry and sends a negative signal to companies seeking to invest in [the country],” the spokesperson told BioSpace via email.
Indeed, Boehringer Ingelheim and Eli Lilly in June scrapped plans to invest about €2 billion ($2.2 billion) in Germany in response to proposals to cut healthcare spending.

Roche sees a “practical and effective” version of the recently proposed site-exemption clause as the last chance to “restore confidence in Germany as a competitive and reliable investment location,” the spokesperson said. The proposals must become a workable law at the start of next year to achieve that goal, the spokesperson added.
Recent healthcare reforms will, starting Jan. 1, 2027, increase a mandatory manufacturer discount on branded medicines from 7% to 15.5%. A German government committee presented a clause late last month, however, that would allow companies meeting criteria tied to investing in Germany to receive reductions in that mandatory rebate. The new policy, if enacted, could incentivize biopharma companies to invest in R&D and manufacturing in Germany, but it is unclear whether the clause will fully address the industry’s concerns.
“Such a clause will only be credible if it forms part of a broader economic policy agenda that rewards innovation, provides predictable framework conditions for investment and restores Germany’s international competitiveness,” the Roche spokesperson said.
The policy proposal could affect billions of dollars of investment. In addition to Boehringer and Lilly’s withdrawn investments, Roche has a significant presence in Germany. PARIS — France and the United Kingdom carried out a joint airborne nuclear strike exercise for the first time, with Eurofighter Typhoon jets from the Royal Air Force escorting French Rafale jets on a simulated nuclear-strike mission.
The French and British fighter jets flew a joint mission on Tuesday during the exercise Rummy, the French Armed Forces Ministry said in a statement on Friday, calling the drill a show of growing cooperation in the framework of an agreement last year for closer nuclear cooperation and coordination between the two countries.
France is working with several European allies on a concept of “forward deterrence” amid uncertainty around United States security guarantees for Europe in the face of an aggressive Russia. While both France and the U.K. operate strategic ballistic-missile submarines as a nuclear deterrent, France has an airborne component, which the U.K. lacks, in the shape of Rafale jets carrying nuclear-tipped cruise missiles.
“Having independent nuclear forces doesn’t exclude coordination,” French Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin said. “By coordinating, our nuclear forces demonstrate that they can contribute even more significantly to the overall security of the alliance and the peace and stability of the Euro-Atlantic zone.”
The British aircraft operated alongside those of France’s Strategic Air Forces over the Mediterranean, with Typhoons escorting Rafale fighters, according to the ministry. While the Rafale jets performed a simulated nuclear strike, the exercise didn’t involve any actual nuclear weapons, the ministry said.
In addition to Eurofighter Typhoon and Rafale jets, the exercise included A330 MRTT tanker aircraft, French Armed Forces Chief of Staff Gen. Fabien Mandon said in a post on the social network X. The French and British crews took off from Saint-Dizier air base in northeastern France, and showed a “very high level of interoperability and a capability to coordinate,” he said.
Mandon’s post included a picture showing three taxiing Eurofighters, as well as a Eurofighter under a hard cover with the markings of the RAF 29 Squadron.
“This is a revolution for the Strategic Air Forces, which have always operated in complete autonomy since their creation in the 1960s,” said Etienne Marcuz, a senior analyst at the Fondation pour la Recherche Stratégique, in a post on X. He called the involvement of at least three British Eurofighter aircraft “quite significant.”
The exercise was an important step in the implementation of the Northwood Declaration , showing a determination to deter common threats together, the ministry said. France and the U.K. last year agreed to deepen nuclear cooperation and coordination, stating in the declaration that they agreed there was no extreme threat to Europe that would not prompt a response by both nations.
The exercise Rummy took place on Oct. 20 and 21, according to the ministry. France’s Air and Space Force regularly holds simulated nuclear-strike exercises called Poker.
The U.K. and France maintain sovereign and independent nuclear forces, and decision-making regarding their use isn’t shared, the ministry said. The countries would only consider using nuclear weapons in “extreme circumstances of legitimate defense,” the French ministry said.

There wasn’t much change in Airbus’ latest 20-year forecast for air cargo. The manufacturer, which plans to begin delivering an all-new A350 freighter in about a year, estimated annual cargo traffic growth would tick down a tenth of a point compared to last year’s report, but that the industry would require a few more planes than previously thought.
Airbus projected that the global fleet of cargo jets will grow 46% by 2045, requiring 2,670 new aircraft — 65 more than in last year’s report. The majority of new freighters will come in the form of replacements for older existing equipment, with nearly 1,100 for growth to accommodate an estimated 3.2% compound annual growth rate in air cargo volumes. Of the total influx, 970 airframes will be factory-built, with 1,700 aircraft entering the fleet as passenger-to-freighter conversions, according to the company’s market forecast released on Wednesday.
A year ago, Airbus said it expected 45% growth in the global freighter fleet, with 2,605 new aircraft combined with 815 existing aircraft. The total fleet estimate in the 2026 report is for 3,460 aircraft, a difference of 40 additional aircraft versus the prior forecast.
Fifty-seven percent of the demand for 2,670 aircraft will be in medium and large widebody freighters used in long-haul and transcontinental transportation.
Airbus based its estimate of 3.2% growth in air cargo demand on economists’ predictions for global trade to continue growing at a steady pace (2.9% per year). Air cargo growth has exceeded growth in global trade for many years, despite geopolitical, fuel and supply chain turbulence. Last year, Airbus estimated air cargo would develop at a rate of 3.3% per year.
The growth projection is better than the 2.3% compound annual growth of the past 20 years, which included two major global economic shocks. The outlook is better than some expected because the impact of tariffs on air cargo demand has been muted, with volumes shifting to different regions rather than declining.
Asia, a massive hub for industrial and high-tech production, is the fastest growth region for air cargo, at a projected pace of 4%.
Boeing said in its forecast last year that the market would see 2,900 total freighter additions, with the global freighter fleet growing by 67%, including 955 newbuilds, and air cargo traffic growing at 3.7%. Boeing is scheduled to issue its updated forecast next week.
In 2026, air cargo volumes through August were up 4.6% year over year, according to the International Air Transport Association and other market analysts. That’s an improvement from the solid 3.3% growth in 2025, when global trade faced a series of headwinds led by the United States unleashing a series of high tariffs on trading partners, especially China.
The U.S. tariffs on China, including on huge volumes of direct-to-consumer e-commerce packages that previously entered the country duty free, has shifted $750 billion worth of Chinese exports — and air cargo volumes — to other markets since last year. The U.S., in turn, has imported $375 billion from other parts of the world — notably Vietnam, Taiwan and Thailand — more than offsetting the reduction in imports from China. U.S. imports from the rest of the world are up 12% so far this year, according to global trade data compiled by Accenture..
Last year, North American air cargo demand dipped 1.1%. In 2026, Chinese exports to the United States are starting to pick up, influenced by tariff waivers and other factors, helping to push up North American air cargo volumes by 5.9% year over year.
Middle East air cargo volumes have fallen 6.5% year-to-date through August because of the U.S. war with Iran. Connecting cargo traffic through the Middle East is down to 31% versus 38% last year. Europe-Asia traffic is up 3% in that time span as more carriers bypass the Middle East and fly direct between the regions. Central Asia, with transit hubs in Baku, Azerbaijan, and Tashkent, Uzbekistan, has also seen increased growth in freighter traffic.
A big impetus for air cargo has been computers, semiconductors and electronic equipment, which has doubled to 15% of total value from two years ago primarily because of demand by AI hyperscalers to outfit data centers with servers. The equipment is relatively light considering that the high-tech weight share of air cargo is 6.2% and only increased 2.2 points even as demand sharply climbed.
The global freighter fleet has significantly increased to more than 2,350 freighter aircraft in service because the boom in air cargo during the Covid economic crisis led to a spike in passenger-to-freighter conversions and a sharp slowdown in aircraft retirements as carriers held onto assets to take advantage of big market opportunities. Two-thirds of those planes will be replaced in the next 20 years.
“On average, the fleet is a lot older than what it was just five or ten years ago. And that’s why there is a very strong demand for replacement aircraft, whenever they become available. Cargo airlines will decide to phase out their very old aircraft and then to phase in either new aircraft or converted aircraft,” said Francois Cabaret, head of market forecasts at Airbus, during a virtual briefing for reporters.
Freighter retirements increased in 2025 to about 75, according to Cirium.
Cabaret said that most of the demand for aircraft in the 80-ton category will be for new builds because widebody passenger aircraft are flown so many hours during their lifetimes that conversion may not make as much sense, especially with new aircraft that have better range and payload capacity.
Airbus does not have a conversion program for large jets and is incentivized to sell the new A350, based on the popular A350 passenger jet. Meanwhile, new Boeing 777 conversion forms from Israel Aerospace Industries and U.S.-based Mammoth Freighters have dozens of conversion orders as their first freighters roll out to customers.
Airbus does do aftermarket conversions of its A330-300 medium widebody jet and A321 standard airliner.
Crawford Hamilton, head of freighter marketing, was adamant that Airbus would make the first customer delivery of the A350F in late 2027, in line with previous company pronouncements. The A350F last month completed its first initial test flight and is scheduled to undergo nine months of additional flight testing, after which European civil aviation authorities are expected to certify the aircraft for commercial use.
In addition to flight testing, Airbus continuously practices loading and unloading the A350 with different types of equipment to develop optimal operating techniques for airlines to use.
Airbus has 115 orders for the A350 from 14 named customers and one unidentified. Boeing has 81 orders for its next-generation 777-8 freighter.

Beauer X4 Is a Tiny Travel Trailer That Triples in Size at Camp and Makes Room for Everything
35 photos
Photo: YouTube/Caravan TV
A complete living solution in an ultra-compact and lightweight towable, who wouldn't want that? If convenience and compactness rank high at the top of your priorities list, the Beauer X4 might be the best choice: an iconic travel trailer that transforms at camp to make room for everything inside.
The Beauer X4 name is new, debuting a short while ago as a 2027 model.
The Beauer X4 itself as a product is not new: this is the transformable, highly innovative viral travel trailer that was previously known as Beauer 3X . It's been around since 2012, being constantly overhauled and in steady, though limited, production ever since it debuted as a concept. Beauer itself calls it The Icon, and The Icon is back for another round, with a handful of changes.
First things first, though: the change in name. It comes about as French RV specialist Beauer is going through a sort of rebranding, fueled by a change in ownership. With the rebranding comes the expansion they announced in September, culminating with the debut of two brand new models at the 2026 Dusseldorf Caravan Salon.
Photo: YouTube/Caravan TV At about the same time, the flagship Beauer 3X, the first and most famous product Beauer made, was seemingly replaced by the Beauer X4. The more recent 2026 Caravan and Motorhome Show at NEC Birmingham confirmed that the two, the 3X and the X4, are basically the same model, with some improvements and a bit more variety.
The Beauer X4 is now available at select dealers in the UK as well. The most significant upgrade to the original model is the availability of two floorplans: the original one with the L-shaped kitchen and another one, called simply Layout 2, which has a more compact kitchen, a larger bathroom, and a bedroom with space to move around.
We actually stumbled across it in November 2025, when Beauer listed a display unit for sale, and correctly assumed it was a new floorplan. This layout also erases the entire wall of cabinets for storage and creates an even airier, more home-like space.
Photo: YouTube/Caravan TV Further refinements over previous iterations include nicer cabinetry, a wider choice of options for customization, and a longer list of upgrades ranging from solar to e-motors for easy hitching and parking, and AC, composting toilet, and an all-electric kitchen.
At its core, the Beauer X4 remains the same awesome little thing it was when it first popped up as a concept: a round, almost cute travel trailer that takes up very little space behind the towing car or inside the family garage, but which will turn into a family-friendly home on wheels in 60 seconds , at the push of a button.
The mechanism that makes this transformation possible hasn't changed either. The X4 is made of three separate modules that travel stacked one on top of the other and slide outwards at camp thanks to motors fed by a 100Ah leisure battery. Once parked, the trailer triples in width and becomes a complete home, with a lounge/dinette/second bedroom, a kitchen, a very compact bathroom, and a bedroom.
Photo: YouTube/Caravan TV Storage is limited, but it exists in a full wall of cabinets in the central part and some overhead lockers. As with any transformable trailer or RV, storage options disappear so it can transform. As you can see in the second video below, in the case of the X4 , the furniture moves with the modules, being lifted up and tucked over non-movable segments like the kitchen.
The entire composite structure rests on an AL-KO chassis with a single axle and 12-inch wheels, stabilizers, shock absorbers, and a manual step. The 2027 version includes an awning-style flap over the door, which will offer some protection from the elements.
Dimensions remain the same as in the old 3X, so you're looking at a travel trailer that's 3.5 meters long overall and just 1.95 meters (6.4 feet) wide in road mode. At camp, width "grows" to 4.6 meters (15 feet), so you get 12 square meters (129 square feet) of living space.
Photo: YouTube/Caravan TV The kitchen and the bathroom are the fixed parts. The lounge at the back comes with a U-shaped couch that also converts into a double bed and a flip-up dining table that attaches to the main kitchen block. Standard spec brings a two-burner gas cooktop and sink combo, the kind you'll find in most European travel trailers and average-priced campervans, as well as an under-counter fridge and plenty of storage.
You can upgrade it to include a one- or two-burner induction cooktop, add a microwave, or opt for a bigger fridge. You can also customize colors, both for the wood in the kitchen and the upholstery in the living room.
The pass-through bathroom comes with a cassette toilet and a small sink, but you can also add a shower tray and shower kit, so you can have a proper washroom.
Photo: YouTube/Caravan TV The bedroom at the front end features a double bed, some cubbies over the window, reading lights and power outlets. The cabinets mounted in the wall next to the bathroom can be accessed from inside the bedroom as well.
Standard features include a 55-liter (14.5-gallon) tank for freshwater, an outdoor shower with just cold water, and a 6-liter electric water heater. Beauer promises that the X4 is easy to set up and easy to tow, stylish and perfectly comfortable for a family of four or two couples traveling together.
The list of add-ons is impressive, as already noted. There's a Signature Option that brings a custom paintjob, but also more functional upgrades like a Dometic chassis-untegrated reversible AC, the remote-controlled dual-motor mover, 13-inch aluminum wheels, a reinforced insulation kit for extended camping, a Thule awning, a bigger battery and 100W of solar, a 2000W Webasto gas or electric underfloor water heater, a Truma 1800 Eezy electric heater, or a Fiamma bike rack.
Photo: YouTube/Caravan TV Maximum permissible weight is 1,350 kg (2,976 lbs) with about 150 kg (331 lbs) of payload that will have to include your options. Pricing will depend on those options as well, and it starts at €39,990 in Europe and £43,990 in the UK, which would be about $44,800 and $58,800 respectively.

Rupa Is a Sophisticated Camper Van With an Open Layout, Interior Staircase, and a Rooftop Terrace
30 photos
Photo: VannyCampers
For many vanlifers, camper vans are much more than just a mode of transportation. They are true homes on wheels, and as van conversions like the Rupa showcase, they can offer both beautiful aesthetics and modern functionality.
Luckily, there are countless ways to transform standard vans into genuine mobile dwellings, but making the most of the limited space available inside these vehicles often comes down to good design and clever organization rather than adding more features. This is also the design philosophy behind Rupa, and the result is a stunning roving home with an open interior layout, a soft color palette, and practical amenities that make everyday living on the road feel more like being at home.
This gorgeous camper van is based on a 2023 Mercedes-Benz Sprinter LWB with rear-wheel drive and a 2.0 CDI diesel engine. It’s a build designed for weekend getaways, coastal drives, road trips, and paved-road van life, and it stands out with its earth-toned, retro-inspired color palette and a unique interior arrangement that strays away from the popular side kitchen and rear fixed bed configuration.
Apart from that, the camper van incorporates some features that you don’t usually find in converted vehicles, such as an ingenious interior staircase, a rooftop terrace, and a walk-through bathroom. I’ll give you more details about each of them below.
Photo: VannyCampers But first, let’s talk about the choice of colors and finishes in this camper van. Named after the Sanskrit word for beauty and form, Rupa is one of those vans that look and feel like a luxurious hotel room. The interior styling combines understated neutrals with light terracotta/muted pink and green accents to create a cozy and highly sophisticated ambiance .
The star of the space is the Folly Pink shade, a warm, clay-like pink used on the lower cabinetry, the staircase, the framing of the shelving, and the accent walls. It brings a mid-century modern warmth to the space and combines with satin brass fixtures that add another tinge of luxury.
Most of the upper walls, the ceiling, and the upper cabinetry are finished in a soft, warm off-white that keeps the interior bright, airy, and spacious, without feeling sterile. Bespoke light green upholstery, an oak-effect flooring, and white stone-like countertops complete the interior design. Overall, the compact living space feels luxurious, relaxed, and full of character.
Photo: VannyCampers The rather uncommon layout showcases efficient use of space. There is no fixed partition wall between the driver’s cabin and the actual living area, and the double passenger seat swivels to provide extra seating at camp. At the front, a four-seater built-in sofa constitutes the lounge area, the central section of the van is occupied by a dual-sided kitchen, and at the rear, there is a walk-through wet bathroom.
When it comes to sleeping arrangements, Rupa can accommodate up to four travelers thanks to the convertible sofa that transforms into an extra-long bed measuring 189 x 137 cm (74 x 54 inches) and an additional bed in the pop-top. A removable table is also included. It can be mounted in front of the sofa to provide a practical space for dining or working on the road.
The distinct functional areas seamlessly flow into each other, and overhead storage integrated throughout the van makes it easy to keep personal belongings organized and the living space uncluttered.
Photo: VannyCampers One of the most eye-catching features inside Rupa is the staircase leading from the living area to the roof terrace. Rather than standing as a separate staircase, it seamlessly integrates into the kitchen design, providing additional storage. It’s also finished in the same shade of pink as the cabinetry, so it blends in perfectly.
This staircase leads to a hatch that opens onto the pop-top roof. This mezzanine area houses a 200-by-118-cm (79-by-46-inch) bed, perfect for one or two children. It comes with a panoramic canvas with zip-up windows and fly screens for proper ventilation.
Adjacent to it is another standout feature - a wooden roof deck that offers a nice, elevated place to spend time outside and take in the surrounding views.
Photo: VannyCampers Returning inside, the kitchen is quite spacious for a camper van . The dual-sided layout means there is ample counter space for meal prep, while modern appliances ensure modern functionality. The cooking equipment consists of a two-burner induction stove and a microwave, and the van is also equipped with a sink and a 58-liter Alpicool compressor fridge. A Truma D4E system provides hot water.
The rear bathroom is separated from the rest of the living area through a sliding door and is fitted with two white shower screens, stone-effect wall finishes, and a black mixer shower. A small matching sink and a Thetford 565 toilet are also included in this space for added convenience.
Photo: VannyCampers Though this camper van is not intended for adventurous off-road journeys, it does allow for extended trips away from the city or campsites. It is equipped with a 628Ah lithium battery bank that works in conjunction with 300W of solar panels on the roof and a 3,000W Renogy inverter charger. An external electrical hookup is also included. The electrical system components are housed in a dedicated compartment next to the rear bathroom, and garage storage is available above it.

This Guy Has Been Working for Ford for 60 Years, Has Tools Older Than His Workmates
8 photos
Photo: Ford From the Road
The first time Eddie O'Brien walked through the gates of the Ford Dagenham plant, back in 1966, he was a 16-year-old apprentice. Fast forward to 2026, and he has just celebrated 60 years with the company with no interruption whatsoever.
Eddie O'Brien has been with Ford through 13 different Prime Ministers. Back when he started, England had just won the World Cup, something it has not done again since. The world has changed over the years, but one thing has remained the same. Eddie showed up for his shift, day or night.
His own celebration in 2026 coincides with a major anniversary for his workplace. The event that marked his six-decade-long career with Ford took place exactly 95 years after the Ford Dagenham site started operating.
Dagenham is now a major powertrain hub, producing high-volume diesel engines, such as the 2.0-liter EcoBlue, for Ford’s global commercial vehicle lineup. But for 71 years, the manufacturing facility was a massive vehicle assembly facility, rolling out over 11 million cars, trucks, and tractors, including models such as the Cortina , Capri, and Fiesta. Vehicle assembly officially ceased at the site in 2002, when the final UK-built Ford Fiesta rolled off the production line.
Photo: Ford From the Road For him, the Blue Oval adventure started with the Ford Trade School, doing what they called a sandwich course. At the time, he actually applied for three jobs. One was at a rubber factory in Essex, and another was with British Gas. But he wanted to work for Ford the most, so here he is, 60 years later.
He began training at the specialized company trade school located in nearby Harold Hill. Upon entering the main Dagenham complex, he was first deployed to the River Plant. He later transitioned to the facility’s Central Repair Garage to sharpen his mechanical expertise.
In 1973, he found his permanent home within the company. For over five decades, he has worked specifically as a Mechanical Maintenance Craftsman. His primary responsibility has been maintaining the massive infrastructure required to handle vehicle logistics, keeping heavy industrial machinery, site tugs, and locomotives running smoothly.
Many refer to the machine shop where he spends most of his time as "Eddie's Shop." It is where he does his job and has tools older than some of his current workmates. He bought them himself ages ago. He remembers that he paid 5 pounds for a micrometer to gauge small distances and thickness. That was a week’s wages at the time. He remembers he and his colleagues were paid in cash back then.
Photo: Ford From the Road There are photos of him in black and white up on the walls, showing different stages of his career. Eddie credits his incredible work longevity in a demanding blue-collar career to his lifetime dedication to physical health, particularly his love for cycling and taking part in charity bike rides. He took up cycling about 24 years ago and hasn't stopped since.
He only wished he'd started sooner. If he had, he would have ridden more than the few 100-mile races that he has completed so far. He still does it, usually in the company of one of his sons outdoors or by himself, indoors. " I do like to push it, get my blood pumping ," he says.
He also takes his grandchildren cycling every once in a while. Staying active is probably one of the reasons he hasn't gained weight over the years. He also took up running ten years ago but had to stop after he injured his foot.
He is well aware that now, his time at Ford is inching closer to the end due to the physical demands of the job and admits that " 60 years is a nice number to sign off on ." " I think some of the younger guys do look after me a little bit. Not too much, " he says.
Photo: Ford From the Road The best part of his job? He got to work on and for some iconic vehicles. For instance, he had to make jigs for some repairs for the Le Mans Ford GT40 at the Heritage Center as fast as he could because they needed them for a TV show. As a reward, he received a plaque with one of the pistons from the blow-up engine on it.
He has been a Ford owner over all these years. He drives a Fiesta now, but he has had Cortinas, other Fiestas, and even Transits, along with a Sierra, which he affectionately calls his favorite. However, he has always been in love with motorcycles. He has even raced them until 1988. He has recently sold his Kawasaki 500 Enduro that he used to ride to work every day, regardless of the weather. All of a sudden, he no longer enjoyed it, so he got rid of it.
Once he retires, he plans to focus on cycling and spending time with his family, especially with his grandchildren and great-grandchildren. He wasn't even planning to start a family in the near future when he started working for Ford.
